chapter_theme: Ainkurunuru 441 to 450, Peyanar's mullai decade of the war camp (பாசறைப் பத்து): the married man in the king's camp in the rains, longing for his wife, wishing she knew his pain, picturing her as hostess of guests and mother of his son, and making every return hang on one condition, if the king's work ends.

441.reading: In the war camp the man says that the words of his red-complexioned wife have become a thing of wonder to him, for he left her helpless on a day of the rains with its thunder, and they now give him real pain; it would be well if she knew the sorrow he suffers.
441.nuance: The pain runs the other way from the usual mullai poem: it is her parting words that wound the man, and his wish is not to see her but that she should know his suffering, a defence against the charge of neglect.

thinai_evidence.note: parting on a day of the rains, the mullai season

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (பாசறைப் பத்து) places the man in the king's war camp; he speaks to himself

442.reading: If the fierce king's hard campaign subsides, the man says, his wife will be fit to receive guests in plenty, she whose chastity is like Arundhati's in the high world of the dark sky, the mother of a son who wears a gem ornament shaped like a young palm fruit.
442.nuance: Homecoming is pictured not as embrace but as the household's hospitality restored: the wife's role as hostess of guests waits on the king's war.

thinai_evidence.note: the man waits on the end of the king's war to return home

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (பாசறைப் பத்து) places the man in the king's war camp; no addressee is named

443.reading: If the king, whose earth-smeared drum has taken many forts rising to the sky, leaves off his work, the man says, then without calling the way too long he will mount the good chariot and go to see her lovely bright brow, like the young crescent of the shining moon.

thinai_evidence.note: the return hangs on the king's work ending

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (பாசறைப் பத்து) places the man in the king's war camp; no addressee is named

444.reading: We shall see the simple girl of broad shoulders, the man says, if the king of the victorious spear, his enmity calmed, may yet head back to his own land, the king whose great-tusked elephants have split their tusk-rings and blunted their sharp points charging the long walls of forts.
444.nuance: The blunted tusks measure how long the siege has lasted: the elephant's wear is the man's waiting made visible.

thinai_evidence.note: the man waits for the king's war to end

iraicchi.act: the young cow comes home at evening keeping close to the bull
iraicchi.sense: even the cattle go home together at dusk while the man stays in the camp away from his wife

445.reading: The man tells his heart, which weeps each time it remembers her at the hour when the young cow comes home close by the good bull, that it left the famed and excellent beloved to lament and came to this camp of hard work, and has quickly drawn him to come as well.
445.nuance: The cattle going home together at evening are what the camp-bound man sees, and they set off the heart's weeping; the poem blames the heart both for leaving her and for its present grief.

thinai_evidence.note: the hour the cattle come home, the mullai evening

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (பாசறைப் பத்து) places the man in the king's war camp; the second-person verbs and நெஞ்சம் suggest he speaks to his heart, though the addressee is not certain

446.reading: The man tells his dark wife, absent, that they will see good things when, having helped the hard work of the war camp, they come back to their beloved good country, and her mullai-scented hair breathes its fragrance.

thinai_evidence.note: mullai in the hair and the war camp

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (பாசறைப் பத்து) places the man in the king's war camp; he calls on her (மாஅயோயே) though she is far away

447.reading: May the king's work be released from its bond, the man prays, and then they will see the bright brow worthy of song, at the hour when the winged bee works open the red bud, shaped like a kingfisher's beak, of the thalavu that grows in the dew.
447.nuance: The bee prising open the jasmine bud is the evening of the rains and may hint at the reunion he waits for; it carries no act of the lovers, so it is scene, not iraicchi.

thinai_evidence.note: the wild jasmine of the forest in flower

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (பாசறைப் பத்து) places the man in the king's war camp; no addressee is named

448.reading: The drum of deep voice sounds in the morning and the fierce king has taken up his work; the mullai blooms at the edge of the soft low field and the rains with thick heavy drops have come; and, the man says, thinking each time of her with her few fine tresses, he has met sleepless anguish.
448.nuance: Three parallel clauses end on the same verb (எதிர்ந்தனனே, எதிர்ந்தன்றே, எதிர்ந்தனமே): the king meets his war, the season meets the land, the man meets sleeplessness, so the war and the rains arrive together as his double trial.

thinai_evidence.note: the rains come and the mullai blooms

thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (பாசறைப் பத்து) places the man in the king's war camp; no addressee is named

449.reading: The chariot is ready and strongly made, its wheels rolling so that the gravel ground breaks, yoked to strong horses weary of standing in the stall; we shall see her bright brow, the man says, if the king finishes his work.
449.nuance: Everything is ready but the king: the horses tired of the stall share the man's impatience.

thinai_evidence.note: the return waits on the king's work

450.reading: May the glorious king, his enmity calmed after the hard work where drums beat in turn, think of his own land, the man prays, so that his eyes may sleep on the young breasts of his red-complexioned wife and the sickness of his hot sighs abate.

thinai_evidence.note: the man waits for the war's end to sleep beside his wife

links.note: Both men in the war camp turn on the wife's ignorance of their pain: Akananuru 304 says she does not know it (நந்நோய் தன்வயின் அறியாள்), Ainkurunuru 441 wishes she knew it (அவள் அறியினோ நன்றே).
links.teaches: Akananuru 304 spells out what the wife who does not know will think, that the man is without right or grace, so the bare wish of 441 is revealed as the soldier's answer to an imagined accusation of neglect.

links.note: Both set the home feast against the king's war: the couplet says let the king fight and win and let us feast at evening; 442 says if the king's war subsides she will receive guests in plenty.
links.teaches: The poem names whose feast the couplet's விருந்து is, the wife as hostess of guests and mother of a son, so the couplet's private wish is shown to be the restoration of a whole household that the king's war holds in suspense.

links.note: Both end on the same conditional of the camp: the king's elephants with tusk-rings split on enemy forts, and 'if the fierce king releases us' (வினைவிடப் பெறினே / முன்னுதல் பெறினே).
links.teaches: Akananuru 164 sets the fort-blunted tusks after a whole season scene and her regained beauty, while 444 keeps only the tusks and the sight of her, which shows the worn elephant is the paasarai situation's own sign of a war too long, not a seasonal ornament.

links.note: The same deep-voiced drum (தழங்குகுரல் முரசம்) sounds in both camps; in Akananuru 24 it keeps the sword-bearing army awake at night, in 448 the man meets sleeplessness thinking of her.
links.teaches: Read together, the drum that keeps the soldiers sleepless for the king's war is the same drum under which the man lies sleepless for his wife, so the camp's wakefulness is shown to be both duty and longing at once.

links.note: 449 has the chariot and horses ready on condition the king finishes his work (வேந்துவினை முடினே); Kar Narpathu 20 reports the king's work done (வேந்தன் வினையு முடிந்தன) and the road grown pleasant.
links.teaches: The pair gives the two moments of the mullai return, the chariot readied in the camp while the king's work hangs, and the fulfilment when the work is done and the rain-cloud itself seems an army going home.

source_issues: The colophon gives no thurai for any poem of the decade; the speaker and occasion are taken from the decade title பாசறைப் பத்து.
441 line 1: ஐய ஆயின is hard to fix (become wondrous, subtle, or doubtful); the reading is marked uncertain.
445: who speaks to whom is not stated; the second-person verbs (வந்தனையே, இழைத்தனையே) are read as the man addressing his heart, and the verse is marked uncertain.
447 line 3 begins யாடு, the glide of செம்முகை + ஆடு split across the line break; 448 lines 2, 4 and 6 print எதிர்ந் தனனே, எதிர்ந் தன்றே and எதிர்ந் தனமே with the word split.
